summary.text: A square matrix is called diagonalizable, or non-defective, if it is similar to a diagonal matrix.
Equivalently, there is a basis made of the matrix's eigenvectors, and the diagonal entries are the matching eigenvalues.
Such a matrix scales space by a different amount in different directions, and diagonalizing it makes later computations easier.

facts.label: Non-diagonalizable name
facts.value: A square matrix that cannot be diagonalized is called defective

facts.label: Why it helps
facts.value: A diagonal matrix's power just raises each diagonal entry to that power

facts.label: Rotation example
facts.value: A generic real rotation matrix is defective over the real numbers

facts.label: Complex numbers
facts.value: Almost every complex square matrix is diagonalizable

facts.label: Quick test
facts.value: Having n distinct eigenvalues is enough, though not necessary

items.prompt: A 3 × 3 matrix has three different eigenvalues, all in its number field. What can you conclude?

options.label: It is diagonalizable
It is defective
It is a rotation
Nothing at all

items.explain: Having n distinct eigenvalues for an n × n matrix is a sufficient condition for being diagonalizable.

items.prompt: A 3 × 3 matrix has a repeated eigenvalue. A friend says a matrix can be diagonalized only if its eigenvalues are all different. Is the friend right?

options.label: Yes, a repeated eigenvalue always rules it out
Yes, but only over the real numbers
No, but only if the matrix is symmetric
No, distinct eigenvalues are enough but not required

items.explain: Having n distinct eigenvalues is a sufficient condition for diagonalizability, but not a necessary one; the converse may be false.

items.prompt: A matrix with real entries turns the plane by a generic rotation. What can be said about diagonalizing it?

options.label: It cannot be done with real entries, but can with complex ones
It can always be done with real entries
It cannot be done even with complex entries
It can be done only if it has distinct eigenvalues

items.explain: A generic rotation matrix is defective over the reals but diagonalizable over the complex numbers.

items.prompt: What does a diagonalizable matrix do to space, geometrically?

options.label: It scales every direction by the same amount
It shifts every point by the same distance
It scales space by different amounts in different directions
It rotates every vector by the same angle

items.explain: It is an anisotropic scaling: each eigenvector direction is scaled by its own eigenvalue.

items.prompt: You need a very high power of a diagonal matrix. Which shortcut works?

options.label: Raise the sum of the entries to that power
Raise each diagonal entry to that power
Raise only the largest entry to that power
Multiply the diagonal entries by that power

items.explain: A diagonal matrix is raised to a power by raising its diagonal entries to that power, and this extends to diagonalizable matrices.

items.prompt: What do we call a square matrix that fails to be diagonalizable?

options.label: Non-defective
Semi-simple
Modal
Defective

items.explain: A square matrix that is not diagonalizable is called defective; diagonalizable ones are non-defective.
